paragraphs.text: This is a lab study in rats about one behavior: rearing, when a rat stands on its hind legs to look around. It asks whether hippocampal activity during those moments is needed to form spatial memories.

sentences.text: This is a lab study in rats about one behavior: rearing, when a rat stands on its hind legs to look around.
It asks whether hippocampal activity during those moments is needed to form spatial memories.

paragraphs.text: Most research on how the hippocampus builds spatial memory looks at walking or quiet rest. Rearing comes with strong 7–12 Hz theta rhythms, which are tied to memory, yet its role in spatial memory was unknown.

sentences.text: Most research on how the hippocampus builds spatial memory looks at walking or quiet rest.
Rearing comes with strong 7–12 Hz theta rhythms, which are tied to memory, yet its role in spatial memory was unknown.

paragraphs.text: A 3D camera detected rearing and switched on a laser that silenced the dorsal hippocampus, using a light-sensitive protein added to its neurons. This was done only while rats learned which maze arms they had visited. Silencing during rearing cut test accuracy from 77.7% to 65.7%, and rats needed more arm visits to find all rewards. Silencing delayed by 6 seconds gave no significant drop, and light alone did nothing in control rats.

paragraphs.text: The authors conclude that hippocampal activity during rearing is important for spatial memory. They suggest rearing may be when the brain updates its internal model of the surroundings.

fuller.text: This experimental study asks whether the hippocampus must be active while a rat rears up on its hind legs for the rat to form a spatial memory. The authors silenced the dorsal (upper) hippocampus only during rears, in a closed loop where detected behaviour triggered the manipulation in real time.

fuller.text: Most research on how the hippocampus supports spatial memory looks at moving and at quiet rest, such as grooming or eating. Rearing is different: the animal stops and actively samples its surroundings, and it comes with strong 7–12 Hz theta rhythm, a brain wave tied to memory. Yet whether rearing matters for spatial memory was unknown.

sentences.text: Most research on how the hippocampus supports spatial memory looks at moving and at quiet rest, such as grooming or eating.
Rearing is different: the animal stops and actively samples its surroundings, and it comes with strong 7–12 Hz theta rhythm, a brain wave tied to memory.
Yet whether rearing matters for spatial memory was unknown.

fuller.text: Rats first saw four open arms of an eight-arm maze, waited four minutes, then had to find food in the other four arms. A ceiling depth camera spotted rears and switched on a laser, which silenced neurons carrying halorhodopsin, a light-driven pump that shuts cells down. Silencing happened only in the first phase, either during rears or 6 seconds after them for the same length of time.

fuller.text: Silencing during rears cut accuracy on the first four choices from 77.7% to 65.7% and raised arm entries from 5.1 to 6.5. Delayed silencing caused no significant drop in accuracy and only a trend in entries, though it still overlapped about 35.5% of rearing. Control rats without halorhodopsin showed no effect in any condition.

brief.text: While exploring, rats often stop and rear up on their hind legs to look around. Research has focused on the hippocampus during walking and rest, not during rearing. This experiment asked whether hippocampal activity while rearing matters for remembering places. Light pulses silenced the dorsal (upper) hippocampus only while rats reared, as they learned a maze.
